overview: Farmers barely react to the AI Plateau and stay fairly relaxed under Steady Disruption and AGI by 2036, where most simply carry on, learn the tools, save and plan around family. AGI by 2028 is the one that frightens them: worry jumps to 3.5 out of 5, and most cut spending and look to family, church, unions or the state for help. Across every scenario, farmers who adapt easily and have money behind them stay calmest, while those who resist change or have little saved worry most.

S0.headline: Almost every farmer stays calm and carries on as before, treating AI as a handy tool for paperwork and records rather than a threat.

whatTheyDo.text: Nearly all of them keep farming exactly as now, with the same herd, the same seasons and the same plans, such as asking for more calving work or a few extra winter hours.
About four in ten keep picking up the useful bits of AI, like using an app for flock records, spray timing or grant forms, and some learn to fly drones.
About a third keep putting money aside, often for a wedding, a house deposit or a tenancy, at something like a hundred to two hundred and fifty a month.
About one in eight spend on the farm itself, for example buying more ewes, a better lambing shed or a neighbour's rough ground, instead of waiting for robots.
About one in ten start or grow something on the side, most often weekend drone spraying or mapping for neighbouring farms.

S0.whatTheySay: Most say they're not surprised, because farming has heard big promises from machinery firms before, and that the tools are useful but not magic.
S0.whatTheyThink: Privately many are relieved that their job stays the same, though some are a little let down that no robot comes to take the back-breaking work, such as weeding. Several point out that their real problem, low pay or thin margins, hasn't changed.
S0.howTheyFeel: Calm, often with a slightly flat feeling, like rain that never comes.

differences.text: Worry is the same for everyone, but adaptive farmers are far more likely to keep learning AI tools (91%) than steady ones (38%), while none of the resistant farmers do.
Younger farmers save more: 43% of those early in their careers put money aside, against 21% of those near the end.
Farmers lower down the ladder save more too: 40% of those in junior roles do, against 19% of those in senior roles.

quotes.name: Daria Zhang
quotes.text: AI was supposed to take my job and it's still me picking up eggs at six in the morning.

quotes.name: Priya Mensah
quotes.text: I'd swap every clever app on my phone for one robot that can weed a carrot bed without killing the carrots.

quotes.name: Uma Petrov
quotes.text: If AI is only hype, I'm still two weeks from broke, it just isn't the computer's fault.

S1.headline: Most farmers are a little uneasy but not scared, and they learn the new kit slowly once they've seen it work on someone else's farm.

whatTheyDo.text: More than half set out to learn the new tools, often by asking the manager if they can be the one trained on the camera grader or the robot milker.
Four in ten hold back until a machine has survived a winter on a farm like theirs, then decide whether to learn it.
About a third push for trials of robots on their own farm, such as a robot mower, lameness cameras or a weeding robot, and offer to run them.
Around three in ten build up savings, for example moving a cushion from two months of costs towards four.
Just over a quarter turn to the union or co-op, pushing for a written deal on paid training and no job losses before any robot is bought.

S1.whatTheySay: Most take a practical line: change is coming slowly, it's part of farming, and people should adjust sensibly. Those who are worried add that workers need a say before the machines arrive.
S1.whatTheyThink: Privately, farm workers in junior roles expect to be the first to go if a robot milker or feeder comes in. Owners and keen adopters see a chance to get ahead, while others doubt the robots will cope with a wet hill in February.
S1.howTheyFeel: Mostly calm or uneasy, a low background worry rather than fear. A few who want to adopt the tools feel excited.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.2 among resistant farmers to 1.0 among adaptive ones. Adaptive farmers almost all push for automation (95%), while most resistant ones just keep going (62%) and wait and see (60%).
Progressive farmers turn to the union or co-op far more than anyone else: 84% of them take collective action.
Worry falls from 1.9 for farmers with thin savings to 1.5 for those with strong savings.

quotes.name: Yusuf Silva
quotes.text: If Martin buys a milking robot, the person he doesn't need is the junior who's still learning, and that's me.

quotes.name: Aaron Ziegler
quotes.text: I'd rather be the man who owns two robots than the man who works next to one.

quotes.name: Emeka Nakamura
quotes.text: I didn't spend twenty-two years learning cows to babysit a beeping box.

S2.headline: Most farmers are alarmed by AGI arriving in two years, and they cut spending hard and look to family, church, unions or the state to get through.

whatTheyDo.text: Two thirds cut back at once, going through every bill, selling a second car or cancelling holidays and the TV package.
More than half plan to lean on others, such as moving in with parents, using the church, asking the bank for a payment break or signing up for public support.
About a third hold on to cash, for example stopping a house hunt and keeping the deposit as an emergency fund.
About a third get political, writing to their member of parliament or pressing the council for a plan and income support.
Just over a quarter join union campaigns and marches, often asking for a fund for workers pushed out or a pause on ending tenancies.

S2.whatTheySay: Most say it's far too fast and that the government has to keep people afloat while it settles, even many who don't usually want big government.
S2.whatTheyThink: Privately many think their job or farm would be gone within a year, and that savings, a tenancy plan or a house plan built up over years would vanish. Farmers who usually watch neighbours try something first say there's no one left to watch.
S2.howTheyFeel: Anxious or alarmed, with many losing sleep. A small number feel panicked, as if the floor has gone.

differences.text: Worry rises from 3.0 for farmers with strong savings to 3.9 for those with thin savings, who also cut spending (84%) and seek support (79%) far more.

Worry rises from 2.8 among adaptive farmers to 4.1 among resistant ones. Adaptive farmers look for side income (54%) and automate (49%), while resistant ones mostly seek support (80%) and cut spending (79%).
Progressive farmers turn to politics (86%) and collective action (81%), while traditional farmers lean on family and church (73% seek support) and make family plans (36%).

quotes.name: Lena Farah
quotes.text: My whole way is to watch others first. With two years there's nobody to watch, everyone's finding out at once.

quotes.name: Lena Olsen
quotes.text: I've milked those cows twice a day for thirty years, and I'd sell them in a morning to save the house.

quotes.name: Fatima Lopez
quotes.text: We've got land and savings, so we'd land on our feet. Ivan sends money home to his mother, and he wouldn't.

S3.headline: With five years' warning most farmers are still worried, but they use the time to save, retrain and get the family ready.

whatTheyDo.text: About two thirds save harder, often by paying off a car loan early and putting the difference aside.
Nearly four in ten start training for what comes next, such as an agricultural engineering course, robot supervision or a cheese-making course.
A third make family decisions, like putting a house on hold, handing a son more of the farm or planning to let the land.
A third put money into something, such as a second-hand spraying drone, a small cutting room or neighbouring land bought at a fair price.
Three in ten build a second income while still farming, like weekend drone contracting, setting up robots for other farms or butchery for neighbours.

S3.whatTheySay: Most say five years is enough to get ready if people start now, and that training should be set up and paid for early.
S3.whatTheyThink: Privately many think the ending is the same as with two years, but they'd be readier and could make one real change. Those with land and savings see time to buy at a fair price instead of a panic price.
S3.howTheyFeel: Mostly anxious or uneasy, but a worry they can act on, more like watching a flood rise than drowning.

differences.text: Worry falls from 3.2 among resistant farmers to 1.8 among adaptive ones. Resistant farmers mostly save (91%), while adaptive ones automate (69%), invest (68%) and start side income (67%).
Worry falls from 3.0 for thin savings to 2.1 for strong savings. Those with a thin cushion save (83%) and retrain (47%), while those with a strong one invest (49%).
Progressive farmers organise (70% take collective action), while traditional farmers focus on family plans (56%) and investing (49%).
Early-career farmers retrain most (53%), while those near the end worry least (2.3) and lean more on automating the farm (36%).

quotes.name: Ivan Rahman
quotes.text: Two years I'd be a passenger; five years I'd at least be driving.

quotes.name: Aaron Jensen
quotes.text: I'd spend five years helping farms need fewer people, knowing one of the people they won't need is me.

quotes.name: Erik Usman
quotes.text: Everything comes back to whose name is on the deeds.

S4.headline: With ten years' warning most farmers feel only mildly uneasy, and they keep farming while planning around family, savings and a slow handover.

whatTheyDo.text: About half build their plans around family, such as marrying, saving for a child's training or handing the farm over gradually.
Nearly half keep saving, often by overpaying the mortgage so it's cleared before AGI arrives.
Nearly half carry on farming as now for the first few years and plan to learn the robots once they're proven.
A third plan to retrain at a steady pace, for example an agricultural robotics course or a qualification studied alongside farming.
A third invest step by step, buying robots and drones as prices fall or growing a farm shop or contracting business.

S4.whatTheySay: Most say ten years is fair warning and there's no excuse not to be ready, so people should train up, set up co-ops and plan sensibly.
S4.whatTheyThink: Privately many think the end point is the same but it no longer feels like a cliff. Older farmers expect to be retired by then and worry more for their children; a few admit they'd keep putting it off.
S4.howTheyFeel: Calm or uneasy, a background worry with room to breathe, and for some even hopeful.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.3 among resistant farmers to 1.1 among adaptive ones. Resistant farmers mostly keep going (78%), while adaptive ones automate (67%) and invest (60%).
Late-career farmers worry least (1.4) and mostly keep going (69%). Mid-career farmers worry most (1.9) and focus on family plans (70%), while early-career farmers invest (47%) and retrain (46%).
Traditional farmers put family plans first (78%), while progressive farmers lean on collective action (59%).
Worry falls from 2.0 for thin savings to 1.4 for strong savings.

quotes.name: Lena Usman
quotes.text: Two years was a jump in the dark. Ten is a staircase.

quotes.name: Nora Garcia
quotes.text: Honestly, ten years is just longer to dread it.

quotes.name: Jade Novak
quotes.text: Somebody has to remember what a cow sounds like when she's calling her calf.
